newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil business wants another six yrs of Cardoso.
newsitem.headline: Brazil business wants another six yrs of Cardoso.

text.p: Brazil's business leaders are exultant over preliminary congressional passage of a re-election bill and are already relishing the prospect of another six years with President Fernando Henrique Cardoso in office.

In the two years since Cardoso came to power, businessmen say they have seen Brazil begin to transform itself from a closed, uncompetitive and inflation-ridden economy into a global player with huge potential.
"We must continue moving in the same direction as the rest of Latin America and the world," said Joel Korn, president of the Brazilian unit of Bank of America and of the American Chamber of Commerce.
"Brazilian society doesn't want to go back to that horrible period of instability and uncertainty," he said.

On Tuesday Cardoso moved one step closer to winning a second four-year term in office when the Lower House of Congress approved a constitutional amendment allowing incumbent presidents to run for re-election.
Before full approval the amendment still requires a second Lower House vote and passage through the Senate, but analysts say the hardest part of the re-election battle is already over.
With opinion polls giving him over an 80 percent approval rating, Cardoso, a former senator and academic, looks like the far-away favorite to win the 1998 presidential election.
For the business community that translates into six years under a tried and respected leader who is comitted to open up the economy and overhaul Brazil's slow-moving bureaucracy.
"A second Cardoso term means that for the first time in our lives we will be able to plan for the real long-term," said Luiz Fernando Furlan president of meat processor Sadia.

Until recently businessmen joked that long-term in Brazil meant not beyond the next couple of weeks. Running a business meant struggling with double-digit monthly inflation, rocketing interest rates all while fending off interfering government officials.
Businessmen say Cardoso has returned an element of predictability to their lives.
Unlike several failed efforts which preceded it, Cardoso's Real anti-inflation plan has been succesful largely because it was carefully explained to the population before being implemented.

Although businessmen have often expressed frustration at the snail pace at which Cardoso's reform agenda has moved through Congress, many now say they appreciate the value of a more open public debate.

"When Cardoso first came to office we thought that with his huge support in Congress, he would be able to have all the economic reforms approved immediately," said Manoel Felix Cintra Netto, head of the Sao Paulo Futures and Commodities Exchange.
"I now realize this is inevitably a very slow process and that we were far too anxious," he said.

Newspapers reported business leaders played a key role in winning the re-election amendment on Tuesday by travelling to Brasilia and threatening rebel congressmen with cutting off their campaign funds unless they lined up behind Cardoso.
Despite their widespread support for the president, businessmen say they now expect the government to speed up the reform process.
"The setting of priorities has not been adequate," said Furlan. "The government is owing us plenty of accomplishements."
Top of their list is a quick overhaul of the tax system as well as social security and administrative reform.
"Re-election is all very good, but you are going to see a lot more pressure on Cardoso to move ahead with privatization and government reform," said Cintra Netto.
((--Sao Paulo newsroom, 5511 248 5410))
